Saying what happened, on the stream meant for it.

**Khora had no way to write to standard error at all.** Everything went to
stdout, so a program's diagnostics and its answer were the same stream: a
command-line tool whose output you redirected lost its own error messages
into the file. Two independent evaluators building ordinary tools reported
it, and one of them stopped trying to keep the two apart.

[`eprint`] is the primitive that fixes it. Everything else here is the
capability built on top.

## Why logging is an effect

Because everything else that reaches outside is. A function that logs is a
function that writes to a stream somebody else owns, and Khora's whole
argument is that such a function says so in its signature:

```khora
fn charge(account: Account, amount: Decimal) -> Receipt
  with { log: Log, db: Db }
  raises DbError
```

That buys the same three things capabilities always buy. A test installs a
logger that collects into a list and asserts on what was said, with no
global to reset between cases. A library cannot log without its caller
knowing, because the row would say so. And the caller decides the format
and the destination, which is the decision a library has no business making.

`print` is not an effect and says so in its own doc comment; it is the one
that predates the argument rather than the one that refutes it.

## Levels

Five, in the order everybody already knows: [`Severity::Trace`],
[`Severity::Debug`], [`Severity::Info`], [`Severity::Warn`], [`Severity::Error`]. Not
four and not seven, because these are the ones every operator has a filter
for, and a level nobody filters on is a level nobody sets.

**The handler decides what to drop, not the caller.** `Logger::to_stderr`
takes a minimum and discards anything below it. A caller that checked the
level itself would be a caller that has to know the configuration, which is
the thing the capability exists to keep away from it.

## The format is JSON

One object per line, on standard error:

```text
{"timestamp":1757021376817,"level":"warn","message":"retrying","attempt":2}
```

**Because a log is read by a program before it is read by a person.** It
goes to a collector, gets indexed, and is queried months later by somebody
who was not there; a format that needs a regular expression to take apart
is a format that loses a field the first time a message contains a space.
`Log::plain` is there for a terminal, and it is the exception rather than
the default.

`timestamp` is milliseconds since 1970, as a JSON *number*. Milliseconds
rather than nanoseconds because a nanosecond epoch is about 2^60 and JSON
numbers are doubles in most readers, which would round it — the same trap
`std::trace`'s OTLP encoding avoids by sending strings. Milliseconds are
about 2^41 and exact in a double for the next twenty thousand years.

`level` is lower case — `"warn"`, not `"Warn"` — which is what Elastic
Common Schema, `slog`, `zap` and `structlog` all emit, and therefore what a
collector's default level filter already matches.

Attributes become fields of the same object. A field named `level`,
`message` or `timestamp` would collide with the three above; it is written
anyway, last, because silently renaming somebody's field is worse than a
duplicate key that a collector will show them.

## Correlating with traces

A record carries [`Attribute`]s, the same ones `std::trace` puts on a span,
so a caller can attach the trace and span it belongs to:

```khora
log.record(Severity::Warn, "retrying", [text("trace_id", trace_id(span.context))])
```

**`trace_id` and `span_id` are added by the handler, not by the caller.**
A line logged inside an `around` carries the ids of the span it was logged
in, because `std::trace::current` is ambient and per fiber; a line logged
outside every span carries neither, rather than carrying zeros. Nothing has
to be threaded through a signature to make a log line findable from a
trace, which was the whole point of the exercise.

```text
{"timestamp":1757021376817,"level":"info","message":"charging",
 "trace_id":"4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736","span_id":"00f067aa0ba902b7"}
```

Attributes named `trace_id` or `span_id` are still written, after these and
by the same rule as `level` and `message`: silently dropping somebody's
field is worse than a duplicate key a collector will show them.

## Types

### Severity

```khora
derive(Eq, Ord, Show)
pub type Severity =
  | Trace
  | Debug
  | Info
  | Warn
  | Error;
```

How much something matters, in the order everybody already filters on.

`Ord` so a handler can compare against a minimum: `Trace` is the least and
`Error` the most, which is the direction "at least Info" reads in.

**Named `Severity` rather than `Level`, and not for taste.** `Level` is what
this is called everywhere, and it is still the name of the JSON field. It is
also a name a program is likely to have already — and today two modules
declaring one type name is a compiler bug rather than a resolution: the
program compiles and then stops on an illegal instruction at run time. This
name avoids the collision until that is fixed, and should go back to `Level`
when it is.

#### Trace

```khora
| Trace
```

The finest detail, off outside a debugging session.

#### Debug

```khora
| Debug
```

What a developer wants while working on this code.

#### Info

```khora
| Info
```

What an operator wants while the program is behaving.

#### Warn

```khora
| Warn
```

Something is wrong and the program is carrying on.

#### Error

```khora
| Error
```

Something is wrong and something did not happen.

## Effects

### Log

```khora
pub effect Log {
  record: (Severity, String, List<Attribute>) -> (),
}
```

Writing a line somebody will read later.

One operation, because a level is an argument rather than a method: five
operations would be five things for every handler to implement and five
places for one of them to behave differently.

#### record

```khora
record: (Severity, String, List<Attribute>) ->()
```

Records one line at `level`, with whatever structure is attached.

## Methods

### Severity

```khora
impl Severity
```

#### label

```khora
pub fn label(self) -> String
```

The five-character name, padded, so lines align in a terminal.

Padded rather than not, because an operator reads a log by scanning the
left edge, and a ragged one makes them read every line instead.

#### name

```khora
pub fn name(self) -> String
```

The lower-case name, which is what goes on the wire.

Lower case because that is what Elastic Common Schema, `slog`, `zap` and
`structlog` emit, so a collector's default level filter already matches
it without anybody configuring one.

#### severity

```khora
pub fn severity(self) -> Int
```

Where this sits, for comparing against a minimum.

#### of_name

```khora
pub fn of_name(name: String) -> Option<Severity>
```

The level `name` spells, or `None`.

**Both cases spelled out, because `std` has no `String::to_lower`.** It
has `Char::to_lower` and nothing that folds a whole string, so the
alternative was to write one here and get Unicode case folding wrong in a
corner of a logging module. A level name is a closed set of six words, and
listing them is honest about what is actually accepted.

`WARNING` is taken as well as `WARN` because half the world writes it.

### Log

```khora
impl Log
```

#### none

```khora
pub fn none() -> Log
```

A logger that records nothing, as cheaply as possible.

**The default, and it has to be nearly free.** If logging costs when it
is off it gets turned off, and then it does not exist. This reads no
argument and builds no string; with Perceus the list the caller passed is
released at the call.

#### json

```khora
pub fn json(minimum: Severity) -> Log
```

A logger that writes one JSON object per line to standard error, at
`minimum` and above.

Stamped from the real clock. `Log::json_using` takes one instead, which is
what a test wants: a fixed clock makes the output byte-for-byte
predictable, and a log line with a real timestamp in it cannot be
compared against anything.

#### json_using

```khora
pub fn json_using(minimum: Severity, clock: Clock) -> Log
```

`json`, reading the time from a clock the caller supplies.

**The clock is a value here, not a requirement.** An effect operation
cannot ask for a capability — it runs wherever the effect is performed,
not where the handler was built — so this holds the one it was given, the
same way `std::trace`'s exporters hold theirs.

#### plain

```khora
pub fn plain(minimum: Severity) -> Log
```

A logger that writes a plain line to standard error, for a terminal.

The level, the message, then `key=value` for each attribute. For a small
program whose log is read by the person who ran it; anything that ships
its logs anywhere wants `json`.

## Functions

### trace

```khora
pub fn trace(message: String) ->() with { log: Log }
```

The finest detail.

```khora
import std::log::{Log, trace};

fn charge(amount: Int) -> Int with { log: Log } {
  trace("charging");
  amount
}
```

**The handler decides whether this is written, not the caller.** A
caller that checked the level itself would have to know the
configuration, which is what the capability keeps away from it.

### eprint

```khora
pub fn eprint(text: String) ->()
```

Writes a line to standard error.

**The stream is the whole point.** `print` writes a program's *answer*, and
an answer is what `> out.txt` is for. A diagnostic written there goes into
the file with it, which is how a command-line tool ends up silently
discarding the reason it failed.

Not an effect, for the same reason `print` is not one: it is the primitive
the effect above is built out of, and a usage message printed before any
capability is installed has nowhere to get one from.

```khora
eprint("usage: report <events.json>")
```
